summary: Specifies the ARPANET 1822L Host Access Protocol, a successor to 1822 which lets hosts use logical names as well as physical port locations. It replaces RFC 802. Replaced by RFC 878.

eli5.summary: A way for computers to be reached by a name that stays the same even if the plug moves. A newer version replaced this one.

subtitle: Logical names for ARPANET host addressing instead of fixed port numbers

tldr.problem: The ARPANET 1822 protocol required hosts to be reached by their physical port location (IMP number and host number), making it difficult to relocate a host or have multiple hosts share a port.
tldr.mechanism: 1822L adds logical addressing: hosts are assigned 16-bit names independent of their physical location. The IMP translates these names into physical addresses using a centrally maintained table. Hosts declare which names they are using when they start up using a Name Declaration Message.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can move without changing their identity, multiple hosts can share a port, and a single host can use multiple ports. 1822L is limited to C/30 IMPs due to memory constraints, but hosts using 1822 and 1822L can interoperate. Replaced by RFC 878.

facts.value: Hosts 57-63 reserved for IMP internal use

today: RFC 878 obsoleted this protocol in 1986. The 1822L protocol was used briefly on the ARPANET before TCP/IP became the dominant suite, but logical addressing concepts survived in modern DNS and virtual hosting.

sections.title: The Problem with Physical Addressing
sections.content:
The ARPANET 1822 Host Access Protocol identified hosts by their physical location on the network: a 1-bit host number (0-63 per IMP) combined with an 8-bit IMP number. This scheme worked, but created operational problems. If a host needed to move to a different IMP or share a port with another host on a time-division basis, every system that referenced that host had to be reconfigured with its new address. Multi-homing (where a single host uses multiple ports for redundancy or load balancing) required assigning multiple addresses.

RFC 851 specifies 1822L (for Logical), a successor protocol that allows hosts to be addressed by logical names independent of their physical location. A central administrator assigns 16-bit names to hosts, and the IMP translates those names to physical addresses at runtime using locally maintained tables.
sections.eli5: The old way required you to remember which IMP and port a computer was on. If the computer moved, you had to learn the new location. The new way lets each computer have a name that does not change when it moves.

sections.title: Three Levels of Addressing
sections.content:
1822L defines three forms of address. 1822 addresses are 24-bit physical addresses (8-bit host, 16-bit IMP) used by the 1822 protocol; they identify a specific port and remain unchanged. 1822L names are 16-bit numbers that serve as logical identifiers, independent of location. A single name can map to multiple physical ports (e.g., when hosts share a port or a host is multi-homed), and the IMP chooses which port to use based on availability and policy.

1822L addresses are a subset of 1822L names—they are 16-bit values with both high bits zero, allowing direct reference to physical ports 0-56 at IMPs 1-255 (hosts 57-63 address the IMP's internal fake hosts). This allows 1822L hosts to bypass name translation when they need to reach a specific physical location.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to address a computer: by its physical port (like a street address), by its logical name (like a phone number), or by a hybrid address that points to a specific physical port but lets you use the new system.

sections.title: Name Translation and Host Declaration
sections.content:
When an 1822L host comes up on an IMP, the IMP does not know which host it is, because multiple hosts might share the port. The host must declare itself using a Name Declaration Message (NDM), listing the names it wants to use. The IMP checks its translation tables to see which names are authorized for that port, and replies with a list of names that are now effective (authorized and ready to use). A host can change its effective names at any time by sending a new NDM.

1822 hosts on C/30 IMPs automatically get the first name found in the IMP's tables, so they can receive mail from 1822L hosts via their logical name without explicitly declaring themselves. The IMP translates between the different message formats transparently.
sections.eli5: When a computer turns on, it tells the IMP what names it wants to go by. The IMP checks if those names are allowed, and tells the computer which ones it can actually use.

sections.title: Address Selection and Multi-Homing
sections.content:
The IMP can apply three different translation policies to find which physical port to use when sending to a logical name. The first policy tries each mapping in list order until finding a reachable one (most common). The second policy selects the closest port by network routing delay. The third policy uses load leveling, cycling through the list to spread load across multiple ports for the same name.

When a single host is multi-homed (connected on multiple ports), all its names might map to multiple ports. If the host is up on all of them, the IMP may send different messages to different ports, chosen according to the policy. A host that needs guaranteed routing to a specific port can use a 1822L address (which maps to exactly one port) instead of a name.
sections.eli5: When a computer has several doors into the network, the system can decide which door to use based on rules: the first available door, the closest door, or spreading the work evenly.

sections.title: 1822 and 1822L Interoperability
sections.content:
1822 and 1822L hosts can communicate, and the IMPs translate automatically. A 1822 host can send to a 1822L host using a 1822L address (the physical location) or (on a C/30 IMP) via the 1822L host's logical name. An 1822L host can send to a 1822 host using 1822 or via the 1822L address (for non-C/30 IMPs where logical names are not supported). Messages arriving at a host are presented in the format appropriate to that host's protocol.

This bidirectional support allows networks to migrate from 1822 to 1822L gradually. However, 1822L itself is limited to C/30 IMPs due to memory constraints for the name translation tables. Hosts on older Honeywell or Pluribus IMPs must continue using 1822 or 1822L addresses.
sections.eli5: Old computers and new computers can talk to each other. The system translates between them automatically, so you can mix old and new.

sections.title: Error Handling and Host Downs
sections.content:
When a destination host goes down, the IMP's handling depends on whether the sender used an address, a single-mapped name, or a multi-mapped name. If using an address or a name that maps to only one port, the sender receives a "Destination Host Dead" message. If using a multi-mapped name, the IMP attempts to find another effective port for that name and tries again; only if all ports are down does it report an error.

For uncontrolled packets (which bypass the normal connection machinery), 1822L imposes stricter limits on data size (959 bits instead of 991) because the packet must carry its own addressing overhead. The IMP notifies the host of name errors (not authorized, not effective, unreachable) immediately, but may not report lost packets after transmission.
sections.eli5: If a computer goes down, the system tries to send the message to another copy of it if one is available. If not, it tells the sender what went wrong.
